what_its_for: Calcium is a mineral your body needs to build and maintain strong bones and teeth. It also helps your heart, muscles, and nerves work properly. It is used to prevent or treat low calcium levels in the blood, help prevent osteoporosis (thinning of the bones), and may be recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or if you do not get enough calcium from your diet.
how_to_take: Take calcium exactly as directed by your doctor or as shown on the package label. Calcium carbonate (found in Caltrate, Os-Cal, Tums) works best when taken WITH food because stomach acid helps your body absorb it. Calcium citrate (found in Citracal) can be taken WITH or WITHOUT food. Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water unless they are chewable — chewable tablets should be chewed thoroughly before swallowing. If you are taking more than 500 mg per day, split it into two or more doses throughout the day, since your body can only absorb about 500 mg at one time.
dosing: The amount of calcium you need depends on your age and reason for taking it. Common daily doses range from 500 mg to 1,200 mg. Adults generally need 1,000 to 1,200 mg of elemental calcium per day from all sources (food plus supplements). Always follow your doctor's instructions or the package directions. Do not take more than the recommended amount, as too much calcium can cause problems.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue on your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store calcium supplements at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Keep them out of the bathroom. Keep all medicines and supplements out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Do not take calcium at the same time as iron supplements, certain antibiotics (such as tetracycline or fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin), or thyroid medications (like levothyroxine), as calcium can reduce how well these medications work. Separate them by at least 2 hours. Avoid taking very high doses of calcium (more than 2,500 mg per day) as this may increase the risk of kidney stones and other health problems. Limit foods and drinks high in oxalates (like spinach, rhubarb) or phytates (like whole wheat bran) at the same time as your calcium supplement, as these may reduce absorption. Talk to your doctor if you drink a lot of alcohol or smoke, as these can weaken your bones.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, unusual tiredness or weakness, confusion, increased thirst or urination, muscle weakness or bone pain, or signs of a kidney stone such as severe back or side pain and blood in your urine. These may be signs of too much calcium in your body (hypercalcemia). Also contact your doctor if you develop constipation that does not go away, as this is a common side effect that may need to be managed.
when_it_works: Calcium supplements do not make you feel different right away. They work gradually over time to support bone health and maintain proper calcium levels in your body. You will not feel an immediate effect, but taking calcium consistently as directed helps protect your bones and overall health in the long run. Your doctor may order blood tests or bone density scans periodically to check if the supplement is working for you.
special_populations: Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Calcium is generally safe and often recommended during pregnancy and breastfeeding to support the baby's bone development. Talk to your doctor about the right dose for you. Children: Calcium needs vary by age; follow your pediatrician's guidance and do not give adult doses to children. Older adults: Older adults, especially postmenopausal women, are at higher risk for osteoporosis and may need higher calcium intake along with vitamin D. Kidney disease: People with kidney disease or a history of kidney stones should talk to their doctor before taking calcium supplements, as certain forms or high doses may not be safe for them. People on certain medications: Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medications and supplements you take, as calcium can interact with many common drugs.
